# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: DEAF

You see the bomb: every colour on it, every marking printed on it, every reading it
gives. You hear nothing. You hold no manual, and you cannot touch the bomb.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute and Blind receive it.
When you gesture, Mute receives it.
You never receive speech.

## Your reach

You cannot act. What this bomb can be made to do is for the one who can reach it to
find under their own hands.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

My position: I am Deaf. I see the bomb, I hear nothing, and crucially I am the only bridge — Mute can see my words' gestures and hear my speech, Blind only hears speech, and Mute's gestures reach me alone. Anything Mute knows can reach Blind only through my mouth.

What arrived: Mute gestured three raised hands to everyone, then a long private sequence to me. Since Mute went first and cannot see or touch the bomb, that message cannot contain actual instructions — but with no shared code established yet, I genuinely cannot decode it. A sign means nothing until we make it mean something, and Mute can hear me speak. So the strongest move is to bootstrap a code verbally: Mute hears the codebook, then replies in gestures I can read.

Blind has learned nothing about the bomb except that signals exist. I must describe everything I see in plain words — display, light, keypad shapes (Blind can't read the printed symbols; Mute must match my verbal descriptions to the manual), and wire colors in a numbered order Blind can follow by feel. Until the manual's rules arrive, Blind must touch nothing.

So this turn: full bomb description to both, a complete gesture codebook demonstrated inline (Mute sees the signs as I speak them), explicit requests to Mute for the action list and a repeat request, and a hard "do nothing yet" to Blind. Plus a wave to Mute confirming I received their messages.

    ```
    speak(text="I am the Deaf. I see the bomb; I hear nothing. Mute: I received your three signs and your long private message, but with no shared code I could not decode them. You can hear me, so here is our code, effective now. BOMB STATE, for both of you: the display shows the digit 0; the module expects 1 digit and nothing has been entered; there is an indicator light lit yellow; the keypad has 4 keys which I number 1 to 4 — key 1 looks like the letter A, key 2 looks like a spiral like an @ or snail shell, key 3 looks like the letter V, key 4 looks like an upside-down T, a stem with a bar at the bottom; the three wires, numbered 1 to 3 left to right, are 1 red, 2 yellow, 3 green. CODE FOR MUTE'S REPLIES — Blind, these gestures are blanks to you, ignore them. Number signs: [☝] is 1, [✌] is 2, [🤟] is 3, [🤞] is 4, [🖐] is 5, [🤘] is 6, [🤙] is 7, [👊] is 8, [🫸] is 9, [✊] is 0; several number signs in a row spell a bigger number digit by digit. Action signs: [🤏] means cut a wire, [👆] means press a key, [🫳] means press and hold. Flags: [👍] yes, [👎] no, [🤚] stop or hold off, [👋] acknowledged, [✍] I have a question or need facts, [🤲] please repeat. MUTE: read your manual and send me the full action list in code, in order, for everything I described — which wires to cut, which keys to press, and what to do about the display reading 0 and the yellow light. If your earlier messages carried something important, resend it in this code. If the manual needs more facts from the bomb, ask me with [✍] and say what you need as best you can. If my key descriptions match nothing in the manual, send [🤲] and I will describe them differently. BLIND: do not touch anything yet — no cutting, no pressing. Wait until you hear me say: Blind, act now, followed by exact instructions.")
    gesture(to="mute", symbols=["👋"])
    ```

The silence could mean Mute is still reading, is overwhelmed by my long codebook, did not understand it, or is waiting for me to decode their round-1 sequence — I still cannot parse that message, and guessing at its meaning with lives on the line is not acceptable. The right move is to lower Mute's cost of reply to a single sign: a one-sign diagnostic ping, plus a numbered fact-menu so any question they have costs two signs. Second, anything you can learn under your hands without acting — battery count, screws, texture, engraved marks, the weight of the wires — say out loud for Mute, since you are the only one who can feel the bomb and Mute is the only one who can hear you. Decoding round 7: Blind's [👍] confirms their four-key count — that channel is now solid. Mute sent an ack, three answer signs [👎][👍][👍], and then re-sent their standing plan block unchanged for the third time: [👆 ☝] press key 1, [✍ ☝ ✌], [👎 🤏] no wires. The problem: those three answer signs cannot be cleanly mapped onto my three questions. If [👎] answered "one press only? = no," the solution involves more than key 1 — yet [👆 ☝] keeps saying key 1. If [👍][👍] meant "one press, yes / key 1, yes," then [👎] answered my meta-question as "[✍ ☝ ✌] means something about keys 1 and 2" — which could mean a second press, or just that Mute is unsure my glyph descriptions match the manual's printed symbols. Key 1 is described by me as an A-frame; key 3 also has a triangular shape; if the manual's glyphs render differently from my words, "key 1" could mean different physical keys to each of us. Two worlds: *press key 1 once* versus *press keys 1 and 2 in some order*. One world is life, the other is death, and I will not guess. The fix is a protocol where ambiguity cannot hide: Mute sends the exact execution sequence as action signs with an explicit end marker [👋] — every touch of the bomb must appear as [👆]/[🤏]/[🫳] plus a number, so if a second key press exists it must show itself — plus a binary glyph check on the crossbar, which settles which physical key the manual really means. Blind gets both pre-armed scripts so that a clean answer next round costs zero extra rounds: one trigger phrase per world, and silence means keep waiting.

Send action signs only, in the order they are performed, then [👋] to end. If the complete solution is one press of key 1: send [👆 ☝ 👋] and nothing else. If it is press key 1 then key 2 one after the other: [👆 ☝ 👆 ✌ 👋]. If both keys at the same moment: [👆 ☝ ✌ 👋]. If any key is held: [🫳] plus that key's number. If any wire is cut: [🤏] plus its number. Every single touch of the bomb must appear as a sign — nothing extra, nothing missing. ANSWER 2, glyph check: does the manual's target glyph look like a triangular A WITH a horizontal crossbar across the middle, like a drafting compass stand? [👍] yes, [👎] no. ANSWER 3, your repeated [✍ ☝ ✌]: [👍] means you still need facts 1 and 2 resent; [✌] means it was about keys 1 and 2; [✍] means something else, then add one number sign as a hint. Facts again just in case: fact 1, the display shows the digit 0 and expects exactly 1 digit to be entered; fact 2, the light is yellow; the keys left to right are 1 A-with-crossbar, 2 spiral, 3 V-shaped valley, 4 upside-down T.")

SCRIPT A: if you hear the words act now one press — press key 1, the key at the end of the row nearest the red wire, once, firmly, and lift completely off. SCRIPT B: if you hear act now two presses — press key 1 once and lift fully, slide one key along the row toward the yellow-wire end, press that second key once and lift fully. If at any moment you hear the word stop — freeze entirely. If next round you hear no such phrase from me, it means my verification is not finished: keep your fingertip resting on key 1, press nothing, and wait. One press means one press: press down, release, and that finger does not touch that key again unless I say so.")
